Northern Cheyenne - It is unlikely that development of the Tract II and Tract III leases would have significant cultural or socio-economic effects on the Northern Cheyenne Indians of the Northern Cheyenne Reservation. The primary reason for this conclusion is the lack of transportation routes, even though the northwest extremity of the Northern Cheyenne Reservation is only about six miles from the southeast corner of Tract III. In order to reach Sarpy Creek from Busby, one must travel west to Hardin and then east to Sarpy Creek, a distance of about 65 miles.
Non-Indian - The town of Hardin is a diverse mixture of ethnic backgrounds which has diffused to the extent that distinct groups are not
apparent. Based on a sample of 72 heads of households, 87 percent were
Anglo, 7 percent were Mexican American, and the remainder were Crow
Indian. Religious affiliations were 62 percent Protestant, 19 percent
Catholic, 3 percent Mormon, and 7 percent "other" with the remainder\nindicating no preference (Westmoreland Resources, 1975 e).
According to local residents, many of the homesteaders in the area were of German or Scandinavian extraction. However, most of the homesteading occurred in the poor economic climate of the 1920's and many of the latecomers failed during the droughts of 1930's, sold their properties and moved elsewhere. As a result, the ranchers now residing in the Sarpy Creek area do not as a group exhibit a distinct ethnic background.
